extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, sociology, and comparative social analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative and descriptive criteria Tocqueville uses to evaluate democratic societies — especially relating to the equality of the sexes, manners, seriousness, vanity, and social organization. Useful for scholars or commentators comparing democratic and aristocratic social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality vs. Sameness between the Sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement does not consist in making beings so dissimilar do pretty nearly the same things; equality should not be confused with making man and woman alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate equality with identical functions for both sexes; preserving distinct faculties and assigning distinct employments better realizes democratic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Duties by Sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the principle of political economy to the sexes by carefully dividing the duties of man from those of woman so that the great work of society may be better carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men handle outward affairs, business, and political life; women manage the domestic sphere and are not compelled to rough physical labor — this separation is held to improve efficiency and social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and Intellectual Elevation of Women
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic improvement for women is raising them morally and intellectually to the level of men while maintaining distinct social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Americans seek to 'raise woman and make her more and more the equal of man' in moral and intellectual worth rather than identical function — this elevation is credited with contributing to national prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of Female Delicacy with Intellectual Strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Women may exhibit masculine strength of understanding and energy yet generally preserve great delicacy of personal appearance and retain feminine manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate women's minds and moral strength without degrading their customary personal manners; strength of intellect and delicacy of appearance can coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal Authority and Democratic Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy's purpose is to regulate and legalize necessary powers within associations; the natural head of the conjugal association is man, and conjugal authority is not to be subverted by democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic society may affirm a head in marital association (man directing wife) while still ensuring voluntary submission and respect — the point is regulation rather than abolition of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary Surrender and Female Pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Many virtuous American women attach a sort of pride to the voluntary surrender of their own will, boasting to 'bend themselves to the yoke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that submission can be experienced as a voluntary, prideful act within the American context rather than coercive degradation; the social meaning of submission matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal Moral Accountability for Seduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans do not maintain a twofold standard of virtue; the seducer is as much dishonored as his victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public morality treats sexual offenses against women with equal severity toward men and women; societal condemnation and legal sanctions reflect equal moral standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Social Respect for Women's Moral Freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans hold woman's honor and independence as precious and protect them vigorously (e.g., rape treated with severity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social mores and laws are shaped to defend female independence and honor; in public, language is guarded in the presence of women and an unmarried woman may travel alone without fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct Private Circles within Democratic Equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite public equality, democracy naturally divides citizens into many small private circles united by similarity of conditions, habits, and tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect citizens to acknowledge political equality yet choose limited private associations; equality in public life does not produce uniform private sociability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistent Personal Pride Produces New Inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when institutions aim at equality, individual pride causes people to seek and form inequalities to distinguish themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation cannot eliminate human desire for distinction; anticipate adaptive, flexible, and often subtle social distinctions within democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of Social Barriers in Democracies vs. Aristocracies
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies inequalities are high, stationary barriers; in democracies they are small, shifting, and often invisible threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social structure, distinguish between rigid class walls and the fluid, ephemeral distinctions of democratic societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Dignity in Manners
rubrics_metrics.description: True dignity in manners consists in always taking one's proper station, neither too high nor too low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess manners by whether they reflect appropriate comportment to one's station rather than artificial pretension or servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic Manners Lack Dignity and Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies manners are generally devoid of dignity and are frequently wanting in discipline or accomplishment because private life is petty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect manners to be less polished and less governed by a shared code; this is a social consequence of equality and fluctuating conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incoherence and Individual Manner in Democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Because no regular code of good breeding can be laid down in democracies, every man behaves after his own fashion and manners are inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging courtesy or etiquette, expect heterogeneity and variability rather than uniform rules; manners will be molded on individual feelings rather than an ideal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of Democratic Manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic manners may be less tutored and less uniform, but often more sincere; the form and substance of human actions stand in closer relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the closer alignment of outward behavior with inner feelings in democratic contexts even if polish is lacking; less superficial imitation of aristocratic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss and Irrecoverability of Aristocratic Manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The light and exquisite touches of aristocratic manners vanish quickly after an aristocracy falls; they cannot be readily recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical change will remove refined mannered habits within a few generations; do not expect a returned aristocratic code of manners once lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic Manners Can Embellish Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not constitutive of virtue, aristocratic manners sometimes embellish virtue and present an imposing exterior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social character, distinguish between outward manners that may beautify virtue and true moral worth; both matter but are distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for Substantial, Productive Pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic peoples prefer pleasures that are productive and substantial — those that mix enjoyment with business — over turbulent aristocratic diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural tastes in democracies favor activities that do not wholly drive business from the mind; leisure often remains connected to productive thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness as a Democratic Habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Free peoples, especially democratic nations, are serious because many citizens are constantly engaged in serious public or private affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious demeanor is a social habit produced by civic responsibility and economic pursuits rather than merely temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent Inconsiderate Actions due to Publicity and Inattention
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic nations, though grave, often act inconsiderately because of an ignorance born of extreme publicity and a habit of inattention — doing many things hurriedly and imperfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect superficiality: citizens prefer to 'know a great deal quickly' rather than know anything well; the habit of inattention is a central democratic defect to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multipurpose Occupations Lead to Imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies the same mind embraces several objects at once and cannot know them all well; this leads to imperfect notions and rash action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating competence, account for the democratic tendency toward multitasking and shallow mastery of many pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Speech and Memory in Democratic vs. Despotic States
rubrics_metrics.description: In large free crowds many words are not heard or remembered, so public men may use imprudent language without lasting compromise; in despotic or silent audiences a few words can ruin a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the risks and constraints on public discourse by the nature of the audience and political regime; publicity can blunt accountability for speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restless and Captious Democratic Vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: American national vanity is restless, captious, and insatiable of praise — citizens constantly seek and demand eulogies and are impatient of censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast this with aristocratic calm pride; in democracies expect active self-promotion and sensitivity to perceived slights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity Rooted in Equality and Precariousness of Advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Because democratic advantages are often recent and precarious, even small trifle privileges provoke jealous pride and ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand displays of vanity as defense of tenuous social gains; the precariousness of status fuels restless self-assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animated but Monotonous Aspect of Democratic Society
rubrics_metrics.description: American society is at once excited (constantly changing fortunes, opinions, laws) and monotonous because changes repeat the same kinds of events: 'the piece is always the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing social dynamism, note that novelty of actors may mask underlying sameness of social patterns and concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Wealth as Differentiator in Democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: With other distinctions (birth, condition, profession) diminished, money becomes the principal means of differentiation; passions end or begin in love of riches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social distinctions in democratic societies by the central role of wealth; anticipate that many social aims will be channeled through acquisition of riches.
